name: Bayeux Tapestry
info: An embroidered cloth nearly 70 metres long, probably commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux and made in England in the decades after 1066, telling the story of the Norman conquest and the Battle of Hastings.

facts.made: Probably commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William the Conqueror's half-brother; most scholars think it was designed and stitched in England, perhaps at Canterbury, most probably by women needleworkers; French legend credited Queen Matilda
facts.form: An embroidery, not a true tapestry: wool thread on a linen ground 68.38 m long and 70 cm tall, in nine sewn panels, 58 scenes with Medieval Latin tituli; the final scenes are missing
facts.where: Normally the Bayeux Tapestry Museum in Bayeux, Normandy; on loan to the British Museum in London from September 2026 to July 2027
facts.known: The Battle of Hastings in 1066; Harold's oath to William; the figure with an arrow in the eye; the earliest known picture of Halley's Comet; a record of 11th-century arms, dress and ships; UNESCO Memory of the World Register

t: The work presents the Conquest from a viewpoint highly favourable to William, and modern scholars generally read it as an apologia for it, though Harold and his soldiers are shown as brave.
Its maker and place of making are uncertain: Odo of Bayeux and Canterbury are the usual view, with Edith of Wessex, Saint-Florent at Saumur and Barking Abbey among other proposals.
It survived the Huguenots in 1562, use as a wagon cover in 1792 and German interest during the occupation, and is the sole surviving example of medieval narrative needlework.
dyk: The last surviving caption, "Et fuga verterunt Angli" ("and the English retreated"), is said to be entirely spurious, added shortly before 1814 at a time of anti-English sentiment.
ev: The tapestry was possibly completed in time to be displayed at the dedication of Bayeux Cathedral
An inventory of Bayeux Cathedral gives the earliest known written reference to the hanging
Bernard de Montfaucon began publishing drawings and a description of the whole work
It was confiscated during the French Revolution to cover military wagons, and a local lawyer rescued it
The Gestapo took it to the Louvre, and Himmler's order to remove it to safety came too late
UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World International Register
It travelled outside France for the first time, on loan to the British Museum

sections.origins:
The tapestry tells the story of the events of 1064 to 1066 that culminated in the Battle of Hastings. King Edward the Confessor of England had no children or clear successor, and succession was decided jointly by the king and the assembly of nobles, the Witenagemot. Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex and the most powerful noble in England, was Edward's brother-in-law; William, Duke of Normandy, was the great-nephew of Edward's mother, Emma of Normandy. The Norman chronicler William of Poitiers reported that Edward had named William his heir and that Harold had sworn to honour this, a claim other sources such as Eadmer dispute.

Narrative hangings were not unusual. Tapestry fragments from ninth-century Scandinavia, such as those in the Oseberg ship burial and at Överhogdal, are thought to stand behind Norman and Anglo-Saxon embroidery. The Liber Eliensis mentions a hanging commemorating the deeds of Byrhtnoth, killed in 991, and English and Norman texts praised the skill of Anglo-Saxon seamstresses. A poem by Baldric of Dol describes a similar hanging in the apartments of Adela of Normandy. The Bayeux Tapestry is remarkable as the sole survivor of this kind of work.
sections.content:
The narrative opens with Edward sending Harold to Normandy. Harold lands in the wrong place and is taken prisoner by Guy I of Ponthieu, then handed to William, whom he accompanies on a campaign against Conan II, Duke of Brittany; near Mont Saint-Michel he saves two soldiers from quicksand. William gives Harold arms, and Harold swears an oath on relics, though the tapestry gives no clue to what was promised. Back in England, Edward dies, apparently leaving the crown to Harold, who is crowned with Stigand, the excommunicated archbishop, in attendance. Halley's Comet appears, a fleet is built, the Normans land, and the battle follows, ending with Harold's death and the English in flight.

The surviving piece depicts 623 human figures, 994 animals, 438 plants, 37 buildings and 41 ships. The central zone holds the action, with scenes divided by stylised trees; the borders carry birds, beasts, fables, farming, hunting and nude figures, and recent scholarship suggests they offer a parallel commentary. Stephen D. White has argued that the fables, drawn from Aesop through Phaedrus, comment on predation and betrayal. Latin tituli name people and places, at times with English spelling.
sections.making:
The work is technically an embroidery: crewel wool on a tabby-woven linen ground 68.38 metres long and 70 centimetres tall, of which about 50 centimetres carry the design. Outline or stem stitch was used for lettering and outlines, and couching or laid work for filling figures, in ten natural dye colours, mainly terracotta, blue-green, dull gold, olive green and blue. Nine linen panels were embroidered separately and sewn together; at the first join the borders do not line up, but later joins are almost invisible. Analysis by the French National Centre for Scientific Research found dyes from madder, weld and indigo.

Scholarly analysis in the 20th century concluded that it was probably commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, who appears four times, possibly for the dedication of his cathedral in 1077. Most scholars place its making in or around Canterbury. Howard B. Clarke proposed in 2012 that the designer was Scolland, abbot of St Augustine's, Canterbury, and Christine Grainge has suggested Archbishop Lanfranc. Carola Hicks suggested Edith of Wessex as patron, George Beech the Abbey of Saint-Florent at Saumur, and Janina Ramirez the nuns of Barking Abbey.
sections.reception:
An inventory of 1476 shows the hanging displayed every year in Bayeux Cathedral during the week of the Feast of St John the Baptist, still the practice in 1728. By the 18th century its art was thought crude, even barbarous. Antoine Lancelot reported a sketch of part of it in 1724, and Bernard de Montfaucon traced it to Bayeux and published drawings by Antoine Benoît in 1729 and 1730. William Stukeley noted it in English in 1746, and Smart Lethieullier's account appeared in 1767.

Its exhibition at the Louvre caused a sensation in Napoleon's time and inspired a musical play in 1804; with the planned invasion of Britain abandoned, it went back to Bayeux. It became a tourist attraction: John Ruskin called it "the most interesting thing in its way conceivable", while Robert Southey complained of queueing to see it and Charles Dickens thought it "the work of amateurs". Modern readers have found propaganda in it, and Andrew Bridgeford has suggested it hides English messages against Norman rule. Historians debate whether the figure with an arrow in the eye is Harold, since early engravings show a spear there, and the meaning of the scene of a cleric and a woman named Ælfgyva is unknown.
sections.survival:
The tapestry survived the sack of Bayeux by the Huguenots in 1562. In 1792 it was seized to cover military wagons and rescued by a local lawyer. A linen backing was sewn on in 1724, scene numbers were inked on it around 1800, and later generations patched it and reworked parts, especially the final scene; the end has been missing from time immemorial. Charles Stothard's facsimile, published by the Society of Antiquaries of London in 1819 to 1823, records it before the 19th-century restoration.

It was stored for safety in 1870 and again from 1939 to 1944. Heinrich Himmler coveted it, and fragments taken from its underside in 1941 were found in 2023 and returned in 2026. The Gestapo moved it to the Louvre in June 1944, but when the SS tried to take it on 22 August Paris was again in French hands. After the liberation it was shown at the Louvre on a 70-metre picture rail late in 1944, then returned to Bayeux in March 1945 and has been on display at the Séminaire de Bayeux since 1983. In 2026 it was lent to the British Museum, despite a petition by Didier Rykner that the journey might damage the fabric.
sections.legacy:
Replicas have been made in many media. Elizabeth Wardle and some 37 women of the Leek School of Art Embroidery stitched a full-size copy in 1885 and 1886, now in Reading Museum; others followed in Canada, Denmark, the United States and New Zealand, the last a half-scale mosaic of 1.5 million pieces of spring steel made by Michael Linton over twenty years. In 2024 the Bayeux Museum bought one of three known surviving Victorian copies. Jan Messent in 1997 and the people of Alderney in 2013 made continuations ending with William's coronation, the subject the missing panels may have shown.

Its strip-like narrative has made it a model for comics: Scott McCloud cited it in Understanding Comics, and Bryan Talbot called it "the first known British comic strip". It inspired cartoons such as John Hassall's Ye Berlyn Tapestrie of 1915, embroideries such as the Overlord Embroidery of 1974 and the Prestonpans Tapestry of 2010, and the work of Hayao Miyazaki, and films such as El Cid and The Vikings have used it in their titles. Historians still use it as a visual record of 11th-century arms, clothing, castles and ships, and it is the first known depiction of Halley's Comet and of a harrow.

summary: The Bayeux Tapestry is a linen embroidery nearly 70 metres long that tells the story of the Norman conquest of England from 1064 to the Battle of Hastings. Probably commissioned by Bishop Odo and made in England, it presents a Norman view of events, yet remains a unique record of 11th-century life and the only surviving medieval narrative needlework.
